lemma Οἴδαμεν γὰρ ὅτι ὁ νόμος πνευματικός ἐστιν; later εἰ ὁ μὲν νόμος ἐστὶ πνευματικὸς, ἐγὼ δὲ σαρκικός εἰμι (NT σάρκινος, some witnesses σαρκικός)
LXX Psalm 18:8 and 18:10; Cyril passes over 18:9; Hebrew/English numbering 19:7, 9
τὴν μόρφωσιν τῆς γνώσεως καὶ τῆς ἀληθείας ἐν τῷ νόμῳ; Cyril: ἔχει τῆς ἀληθείας τὴν μόρφωσιν
ταῦτα γὰρ ἀλλήλοις ἀντίκειται, of flesh and Spirit; Cyril: ἀντίκεινται γὰρ ἀλλήλοις

choices.why: οὐκ ἀγνοίας ἀλλ' ἀπονοίας is a play on words (ignorance / madness); rendered 'not ignorance but reckless folly'.
πνεῦμα in 'the will of the Spirit' is capitalised because the flesh/Spirit contrast follows Galatians 5:17 and Romans 8; the Greek could also be read of the human spirit.
Δεσπότης and τὸ δεσποτικόν refer to God and are rendered 'the Master' and 'the Master’s'.

pass_a_gloss: [Cont. Paul's speech] ... the law given to us for salvation and life (ζωήν), the truly holy and good commandment, became pretext (πρόφασιν) of death to those yoked under (ὑπεζευγμένοις). How or in what way? For if penalty (δίκη) will always follow (ἕψεται) those transgressing law (παρανομοῦσιν), and we have driven on (διεληλάκαμεν) to this [point] of weakness, so as always to be caught (ἐναλίσκεσθαι) in transgressions, [it is] now somehow evident (ἐναργές) that in this way the saving (σώζων) law, the holy and good, seems somehow to have become sinews (νεῦρα) to sin and a road to death to those under sin. [Rom 7:13b] And perhaps, he says, that sin might become beyond measure (καθ' ὑπερβολήν) sinful (ἁμαρτωλός) through the commandment; for to those who have not known (ἠγνοηκόσι) what seems good to the Master (Δεσπότῃ), being caught by penalties will surely follow; for they have done lawlessly (ἠνομήκασι), even if they have not known. Yet there is for them also a not implausible (οὐκ ἀπίθανος) word of defence (ἀπολογίας), I think; for they will put forward (προβαλοῦνται) likely the ignorance (ἄγνοιαν). But for those in law to say they do not know the Master's (δεσποτικόν) will is now somehow vain (εἰκαῖον). Therefore if he should appear having chosen to live impiously (ἀνοσίως), not of ignorance (ἀγνοίας) but of madness (ἀπονοίας) will be the charge (κατηγόρημα), and further of the uttermost lack-of-love-for-God (ἀφιλοθεΐας). So would sin be said beyond measure sinful; for sinner indeed is also the one who has offended (πεπλημμεληκότος) as in ignorance, but least is he said and is [a] sinner beyond measure. [Lemma Rom 7:14a] For we know that the law is spiritual (πνευματικός). He calls the law spiritual as making (ἀποτελοῦντα) spiritual those following (ἑπομένους) it; and spiritual is understood the one not living according to flesh (σάρκα), but rather inclined (ἀπονενευκώς) toward willing to follow the will (θελήσει) of the spirit/Spirit (πνεύματος). And blessed David said: [Ps 18:8, 10 LXX] The law of the Lord (Κυρίου) blameless (ἄμωμος), turning (ἐπιστρέφων) souls; the testimony (μαρτυρία) of the Lord faithful (πιστή), making wise (σοφίζουσα) infants (νήπια); the fear (φόβος) of the Lord pure (ἁγνός), remaining unto age of age. As then he says the law is blameless, for it knows to make blameless, and the testimony faithful as rendering faithful, and the fear pure, for it is purity-making (ἁγνοποιός), so you will receive (ἐκδέξῃ) here too the law said spiritual as rendering spiritual those following it; for even if it is in shadows (σκιαῖς), yet it has the form (μόρφωσιν) of the truth (ἀληθείας). What then Paul? He insists the law is spiritual, but blames (αἰτιᾶται) the nature of man as much sick (νοσοῦσαν) [in] sin; and tries to assure (πληροφορεῖν) that since the law is spiritual, for this reason most burdensome (φορτικός) it is to the nature of man; for what, tell me, he says, if the law is spiritual but I am fleshly (σαρκικός), that is, tyrannised (τυραννούμενος) by the mind (φρονήματι) of the flesh? See how into how great opposition (ἐναντιότητα) of wills (θελημάτων) the things shown set us? For other the will of the spirit/Spirit, and other would be thought that of the flesh; for they lie opposed (ἀντίκεινται) to one another, and have an irreconcilable (ἀσύμβατον) concurrence (συνδρομήν) into identity (ταυτότητα). When then man [is] fleshly and the law spiritual, how would it be bearable (οἰστός) to those so sick [in] sin? And very wisely (ἐμφρόνως); for if he is fleshly, he would be thought as some captive (αἰχμάλωτος) and [cont. u05].
pass_b_english: […] and life, the commandment that is truly holy and good, became an occasion of death for those under its yoke.” How, and in what way? If penalty always follows those who break the law, and we have now sunk so far into weakness that we are always being caught in transgressions, it is already fairly plain that in this way the law that saves, holy and good as it is, seems somehow to have become the sinews of sin and a road to death for those who are under sin.

And perhaps, he says, it was “so that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment” (Romans 7:13). Those who did not know what the Master wills will certainly be caught by penalties, for they have acted lawlessly, even if they did not know it. Yet they have, I think, a plea in their defense that is not unconvincing, for they will likely put forward their ignorance. But for those under the law, to say that they did not know the Master’s will is surely empty. So if such a person is seen to have chosen to live an unholy life, the charge against him will be not ignorance but reckless folly, and, beyond that, the utmost lack of love for God. In this way sin might be called sinful beyond measure. For the one who has done wrong as in ignorance is also a sinner, but he is by no means called, nor is he, a sinner beyond measure.

“For we know that the law is spiritual” (Romans 7:14). He calls the law spiritual because it makes spiritual those who follow it. And a person is understood to be spiritual who does not live according to the flesh, but has turned rather toward the wish to follow the will of the Spirit. The blessed David also said, “The law of the Lord is blameless, turning souls back; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, making infants wise. The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever and ever” (Psalm 19:7, 9). Just as he says that the law is blameless, because it knows how to make people blameless, and the testimony faithful, because it makes them faithful, and the fear pure, because it makes pure, so you will take it here too that the law is called spiritual because it makes spiritual those who follow it. For even if it is in shadows, it still holds the form of the truth (Romans 2:20).

What, then, does Paul do? He insists that the law is spiritual, but he blames human nature as gravely sick with sin. And he tries to convince us that, because the law is spiritual, for that very reason it is most burdensome to human nature. For what, tell me, he says, if “the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh” (Romans 7:14), that is, ruled as by a tyrant by the mind of the flesh? Do you see how great an opposition of wills his words set before us? For the will of the Spirit is one thing, and the will of the flesh must be understood as another. They are opposed to each other (Galatians 5:17), and they cannot possibly come together into one. When, then, man is of the flesh and the law is spiritual, how could the law even be bearable to those so sick with sin? And this is said very wisely. 201 ἡμῖν καὶ ζωὴν δοθέντα νόμον, τὴν ἁγίαν ὄντως καὶ ἀγαθὴν ἐντολὴν, θανάτου
γενέσθαι πρόφασιν τοῖς ὑπεζευγμένοις· πῶς ἢ τίνα τρόπον; εἰ γὰρ ἕψεται μὲν ἀεὶ τοῖς
παρανομοῦσιν ἡ δίκη, διεληλάκαμεν δὲ πρὸς τοῦτο λοιπὸν ἀσθενείας ἡμεῖς, ὡς ἀεὶ ταῖς
παραβάσεσιν ἐναλίσκεσθαι, ἐναργὲς ἤδη πως, ὅτι κατὰ τοῦτον τὸν τρόπον ὁ σώζων
νόμος, ὁ ἅγιός τε καὶ ἀγαθὸς, νεῦρά πως δοκεῖ γενέσθαι τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ καὶ ὁδὸς εἰς
θάνατον τοῖς ὑφ' ἁμαρτίαν· καὶ τάχα που, φησὶν, ἵνα γένηται καθ' ὑπερβολὴν
ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ ἁμαρτία διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς· τοῖς μὲν γὰρ ἠγνοηκόσι τὸ τῷ ∆εσπότῃ δοκοῦν,
ἕψεται μὲν πάντως τὸ ἐναλῶναι δίκαις· ἠνομήκασι γὰρ, εἰ καὶ μὴ ἐγνώκασι. πλήν ἐστί
τις αὐτοῖς καὶ ἀπολογίας οὐκ ἀπίθανος οἶμαι λόγος· προβαλοῦνται γὰρ κατὰ τὸ εἰκὸς
τὴν ἄγνοιαν· τοῖς γεμὴν ἐν νόμῳ τὸ μὴ εἰδέναι λέγειν τὸ θέλημα τὸ δεσποτικὸν, εἰκαῖον
ἤδη πως. οὐκοῦν εἰ φαίνοιτο διαβιοῦν ᾑρημένος ἀνοσίως, οὐκ ἀγνοίας ἔσται ἀλλ'
ἀπονοίας τὸ κατηγόρημα, καὶ τῆς ἀνωτάτω λοιπὸν ἀφιλοθεΐας· οὕτως ἂν λέγοιτο καθ'
ὑπερβολὴν ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ ἁμαρτία, ἁμαρτωλοῦ μὲν γὰρ ὑπάρχοντος καὶ τοῦ
πεπλημμεληκότος ὡς ἐν ἀγνοίᾳ, ἥκιστα γεμὴν καθ' ὑπερβολὴν λεγομένου τε καὶ ὄντος
ἁμαρτωλοῦ. Οἴδαμεν γὰρ ὅτι ὁ νόμος πνευματικός ἐστιν. Πνευματικόν φησι τὸν νόμον,
ὡς ἀποτελοῦντα πνευμα 202 τικοὺς τοὺς ἑπομένους αὐτῷ· νοεῖται δὲ πνευματικὸς ὁ μὴ
κατὰ σάρκα ζῶν, ἀπονενευκὼς δὲ μᾶλλον ἐπὶ τὸ θέλειν ἕπεσθαι τῇ θελήσει τοῦ
πνεύματος· ἔφη δὲ καὶ ὁ μακάριος ∆αυείδ "Ὁ νόμος Κυρίου ἄμωμος ἐπιστρέφων ψυχὰς,
ἡ "μαρτυρία Κυρίου πιστὴ σοφίζουσα νήπια· ὁ φόβος Κυρίου "ἁγνὸς διαμένων εἰς αἰῶνα
αἰῶνος." ὥσπερ οὖν ἄμωμόν φησιν εἶναι τὸν νόμον, οἶδε γὰρ ἀμώμους ἀποτελεῖν,
πιστὴν δὲ τὴν μαρτυρίαν ὡς πιστοὺς ἀποφαίνουσαν, καὶ ἁγνὸν τὸν φόβον, ἔστι γὰρ
ἁγνοποιὸς, οὕτως ἐκδέξῃ κἀνθάδε πνευματικὸν εἰρῆσθαι τὸν νόμον, ὡς πνευματικοὺς
ἀποφαίνοντα τοὺς ἑπομένους αὐτῷ· εἰ γὰρ καί ἐστιν ἐν σκιαῖς, ἀλλ' οὖν ἔχει τῆς

πνεύματος, καὶ ἕτερον ἂν νοοῖτο τὸ τῆς σαρκός· ἀντίκεινται γὰρ ἀλλήλοις, καὶ
ἀσύμβατον ἔχουσι τὴν εἰς ταυτότητα συνδρομήν· ὅτε τοίνυν σαρκικὸς μὲν ὁ ἄνθρωπος,
πνευματικὸς δὲ ὁ νόμος, πῶς ἂν γένοιτο καὶ οἰστὸς τοῖς οὕτως ἠῤῥωστηκόσι τὴν
ἁμαρτίαν; καὶ μάλα ἐμφρόνως· εἰ γάρ ἐστι σαρκικὸς, νοηθείη ἂν οἷά τις αἰχμάλωτος καὶ

review_notes: 'Has rather turned to wanting to follow' was stiff for ἀπονενευκὼς ... ἐπὶ τὸ θέλειν ἕπεσθαι; smoothed while keeping 'the wish to'. American spelling (defense, forever). Psalm 19:7, 9 (LXX 18:8, 10) checked against the verses: correct. Continuity with u05-open ('captive and … in the rank of a household slave') confirmed.
Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf).

The section opens mid-sentence, completing the speech begun in u04-rem-mid (ὥστε αὐτὸν τὸν εἰς σωτηρίαν | ἡμῖν καὶ ζωὴν δοθέντα νόμον), and ends mid-sentence (αἰχμάλωτος καὶ, continuing with Romans 7:14b in u05-open). Both breaks are marked […].
The page number 12 and PG column numbers 201 and 202 in the source block are not translated; the line-break split πνευμα 202 τικοὺς is read as πνευματικούς.
οὐκ ἀγνοίας ἀλλ' ἀπονοίας is a play on words (ignorance / madness); rendered 'not ignorance but reckless folly'.
πνεῦμα in 'the will of the Spirit' is capitalised because the flesh/Spirit contrast follows Galatians 5:17 and Romans 8; the Greek could also be read of the human spirit.
Δεσπότης and τὸ δεσποτικόν refer to God and are rendered 'the Master' and 'the Master’s'.

νεῦρα τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ ('sinews for sin') may recall 1 Corinthians 15:56 ('the power of sin is the law'); possible allusion only, so not cited inline. Likewise ὁ μὴ κατὰ σάρκα ζῶν (Romans 8:4) and τὸ τῆς σαρκὸς φρόνημα (Romans 8:6) are noted as possible echoes only.
